confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 12 other works consulted do not discuss stress.

catalog_locator: Tungoe 2017, Chapter 1, sec. 1.4.2 'Tones in Tenyidie', p. 5
catalog_quote: Tenyidie is a tonal language and has five tones: High, Mid-High, Mid, Mid-Low and Low. Since Roman script is used for orthographic representation, written Tenyidie does not specify what tone to be used, which is based on the context. Meyase (2016) describes the tone system of Tenyidie as a combination of both Register and Contour tones. In disyllabic words, the first syllable has a register tone while the second has a contour tone. However, in a monosyllabic word, it is register tone, for instance the word „Pe‟ can be produced with five different pitches construing five different meanings as shown in the table below. Stress in Tenyidie is realized through elongating the desired syllable while maintaining the tone.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tenyidie/Angami is a five-tone (phonetically four-level) language; no positional or lexical word stress is described. The only explicit remark (Tungoe 2017) treats stress as emphatic prominence realized by lengthening whichever syllable the speaker wishes to emphasize, with its lexical tone preserved. Supporting first-hand observations: Kuolie 2004 (2.1.4, p.34) notes word-final vowels are phonetically longer than non-final ones and lists only tone under suprasegmentals; Meyase 2016 (4.4, 5.8) analyses native disyllables as sesquisyllabic - a reduced, toneless initial minor syllable (pe-/te-/the-/ke-/me-/rə-) plus a tone-bearing final major syllable - i.e. structural prominence is root-/word-final, but he never calls it stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Tungoe's remark is a single sentence without examples or measurements of stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Tungoe's sentence concerns emphatic/pragmatic stress on a 'desired syllable', not citation-form word stress; Kuolie's final-vowel length remark is phonetic and word-level; Meyase's minor/major syllable asymmetry is defined over the disyllabic prosodic word (prefix/minor syllable + root).
new_statements.identity_note: Tungoe 2017, Kuolie 2004, Meyase 2016 and Terhiija 2024 describe Tenyidie = the Kohima (standard) variety of Angami (anga1288, no separate dialect code needed). Chase 1992 and Blankenship et al. 1993 describe the Khonoma (Khwunomia) dialect of Angami; STEDT Monograph 3 has separate Khonoma and Kohima entries.

tone_statements.quote: Angami, also known as Tenyidie, is a low-resource language spoken in the state of Nagaland in India. Angami has four distinct level tones that are represented by numbers. The tones in Angami are T1, T2, T3 and T4, in descending order of f0 height, which correspond to high, mid, mid-low, and low, respectively [28]. … Among the three languages in the current study, only Mizo has tones with dynamic f0 contours.
tone_statements.locator: p. 2, sec. 2.1 'Languages of the current study'
tone_statements.summary: Four level tones, T1-T4 = high, mid, mid-low, low (no contour tones), tone measured on the syllable rime; speech-technology study citing Terhiija & Sarmah 2024 for the inventory; nothing on stress.

tone_statements.citation: Terhiija, Viyazonuo, Zhonei I Gwirie & Priyankoo Sarmah. 2023. Tonal coarticulation in Angami level tones. In: Proceedings of the Second International Conference on Tone and Intonation (TAI 2023), Singapore, pp. 44-48. ISCA. doi:10.21437/TAI.2023-10
tone_statements.quote: Angami is a tonal language spoken by an ethnic group of the same name in the Nagaland state of North-East India. … Considering Angami has at least four level tones and no contour tones, this study provides a unique insight into the tonal coarticulatory phenomena in a level tone-only language. … Angami has four to five level tones. … While some works have postulated the number to be four [13, 14, 15, 16], others consider Angami to be a five-tone system [17, 18, 19, 12]. For this study, we labeled all the possible five tones with the understanding that two of them may overlap (T2 and T3).
tone_statements.locator: p. 44, sec. 1 Introduction (left column para. 1 and right column para. 2); tone labels T1-T5 at p. 45 sec. 2.1; 'register tone language' p. 47 sec. 4
tone_statements.summary: Only level (register) tones, no contour tones: four to five level tones labelled T1 (high, phonetically extra high) to T5 (low), T2 and T3 possibly merged; F0 study of 24 speakers; nothing on stress.

tone_statements.quote: previous literature is divided on the number of tones in Standard Angami and report either four or five tones in the language [22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27]. … Hence, in this study T1 stands for the highest tone, T5 for the lowest tone and T2 and T3, even though these are reported as two separate tones in some of the previous literature, they are considered as a single tone category (T2/T3 hereafter) in this work … In the present study, all the register tones in Angami tend to fall when produced in isolation. The average F0 contours of the five Angami tones are provided in Figure 2.
tone_statements.locator: p. 3971, Sec. 2.1 'Angami and Mizo Language' and p. 3973, Sec. 3.2 'Angami'
tone_statements.summary: Register (level) tone language: five tones T1 (highest) to T5 (lowest), no contour tones; T2 and T3 acoustically identical in the authors' pilot, so four or five levels; nothing on word stress.

tone_statements.citation: Meyase, Savio Megolhuto. 2014. Four versus five: the number of tones in Tenyidie. In: Proceedings of the 4th International Symposium on Tonal Aspects of Languages (TAL 2014), Nijmegen, 13-16 May 2014, pp. 19-22. ISCA.
tone_statements.quote: From statistical analysis, it is seen that there are only four distinct phonetic tones – Extra High, High, Mid and Low. … Though there are only four phonetic tones, morphophonemic evidences show that the phonetic High tone exhibits two forms of alternations. … Hence, there are four phonetic tones and five phonological tones in Tenyidie. … There is only one lexical tone in a non-derived word and only the last syllable bears this lexical tone while the rest bear the default Mid.
tone_statements.locator: p. 22, sec. 4 Conclusion; inventory with examples also p. 19 Abstract and p. 20 sec. 2.2-2.3 ex. 3
tone_statements.summary: Four level tones (Extra High, High, Mid, Low) plus a fifth phonological tone, phonetically High but patterning as Mid (H + floating M); one lexical tone per word, on the final syllable.
